review_text_clean: Absolutely obnoxious. I'm not averse to difficult games, but Devil's Dive is difficult in an annoying way, not an engaging way. Hitboxes are unreadable, environmental hazards are obscured by the viewport, character acceleration swings wildly upon input. The game does not respect your time whatsoever. DD also tries to be a more feature-rich version of Downwell but misses the point that simplicity is one of the things that makes Downwell great. For example, the 360-degree aiming doesn't really add anything to the gameplay, but it does necessitate more awkward controls on a gamepad. Why would a platformer use an aim design that requires migrating the jump command from a face button to a shoulder button? In the case of DD, it feels like the answer to that question is "to be different from Downwell". It is different, but it's not better - I'd say it's actually worse, since using a trigger to jump in any game has, and always will, feel awful. DD looks and sounds great, but, unless you enjoy a very specific kind of old-school, teeth-grinding difficulty, you will not find this game fun. Avoid.

review_text_clean: This game is a shitload of fuck! It's a crusty old fossil reanimated by a mad scientist to reveal it was nothing but a coprolite the whole time! No but seriously, the only thing I could think of while playing was that this is the kind of game the AVGN would get mad at. But unlike the nerd, I don't have to wonder what the developer was thinking; I know he intentionally designed the game to be frustrating, obscure and punishing. The game is clearly a sendup of old adventure games with light RPG elements, like a Sierra/Zelda 2 slurry. And man, it is wildly directionless and inscrutable. You're given almost no guidance, and after two hours of fumbling with the thing I'm still not sure where I was ever supposed to go. Combat is a frustrating mash fest that feels purely random whether you can kill an enemy without being hit in return. Healing is scarce and enemies respawn with each screen transition, so the game quickly becomes a dull slog running back to your bedroom to heal. Significant grinding seems almost mandatory with high item costs. The castle area is annoyingly large with few things to find, leading to most of your time being spent in transit. And God help you if you take a careless step: the princess will happily wander off an edge to her death. The front of the castle is surrounding by an instadeath moat that you must carefully path around or your big, triumphant return will become 20 mintues of lost progress in 1 second. It's a wildly frustrating and unsatisfying game, and the only reason I'm not leaving a red review is because this is a solo dev passion project and I can tell it was deliberately designed to be this way. For a masochist or someone seriously nostalgic for Sierra this is probably a great game. For anyone else, stay far away, especially at $20.

review_text_clean: Similar presentation to Bullet Sorrow, you teleport to next fixed point after taking out enemies that rush in. There's a sequence where you're moving on a crane gantry but most of the time you're standing in the middle of the room. Enemies move to use cover so it's a little frustrating not to have any cover yourself. You're wearing a helmet (there's a HUD in the field of view) so presumably the suit can take a lot of damage and it's possible to dodge incoming fire when the game switches to bullet time. weapons are fixed - an assault rifle and shotgun, reload by pressing the trackpad. Enemies look good and distant enemies are outlined in red so they're easier to see, there's a good sense of size in some of the larger areas. If you like the Bullet Sorrow style of play you'll probably like this. More weaponry with a traditional reload style would have been good imo as would more creative use of cover and the ability to move but that's not what this style of game is about. It's a satisfying blast for $5.

review_text_clean: Robogal is a blend of various puzzles and VN, and all sprinkled with hentai fanservice. An attractive mix (to me) at a budget price. Worth trying, or should you skip it? You play as an unnamed robot constructor, taking orders from clients. Your work requires you to build robot girls based on real women. In order to collect data, you need to locate and interact with target models. Seven women, to be precise. You find them on a city map, where you can click on their pictures. Clicking initiates a VN-style conversation, followed by a puzzle. Puzzles vary a bit. You could be swapping tiles to complete a picture, searching the black screen with a camera to locate your model, mixing colours in a specific order, etc. None of the puzzles pose a real challenge, and the majority can be done in less than 2–3 minutes. After several scenes, you can assemble the bio-robot and move on to another order. There is nothing innovative or creative, but at least there is some variety. Also, after assembling, you can 'test' your creation. Since this is a budget title, my expectations were low. Still, while the puzzles were ok, the English translation sucks. It is better than machine translation, but not by much. Also, the 'testing' option is rather bland. To be honest, for the price asked, the overall quality is acceptable. I was neither satisfied nor disappointed. Just mid. The character art was simply recycled from other games form this dev. I am familiar with most, if not all, of the characters you encounter. Maybe one or two character poses are new; that's it. Moreover, the 'testing' part, i.e., an interactive hentai scene, feels rather lacking. There are a very limited number of very short animation loops. While the quality is fine, I sure expected more. All are uncensored, at least. As for the backgrounds and the UI design, all are fairly good. Similarly to art, the music was also familiar to me. All tracks were present in the other games of this dev. Cost-cutting approach, but the track choices are ok. Nothing catchy or memorable, but they serve their role as background fillers well enough. For the asked price - acceptable. No bugs encountered. To conclude, this game is a low-cost mix of puzzles and badly translated stories. Art and music are fine, but the hentai part is lacking. For a budget price, you get budget entertainment. Only with low expectations is it possible to have fun playing: 4.7/10

review_text_clean: The best way to sum up KOTH is as a first-person, single-piece chess game. The movement is point-and-click, with some limitation. However you wish to classify it, it's a fun game. If you read other reviews or parts of the discussion boards, you'll run across the name "The Sentinel". KOTH is heavily influenced by this DOS game from 1986. Having never played The Sentinel myself, I'm coming into this experience with zero experience. The game is very easy to pick up, but has a slight learning curve. There are 2 modes: Classic and Arcade. In Arcade, you have no limit to moving around. If you can see a square, you can move to it. You will need to absorb trees in order to gain energy to build blocks, which are necessary to get to elevated parts of the topography. While in Classic, in order to move you will first need to place an "Avatar" for your character, then possess and snap to that space where you avatar once was. This is a much more challenging version of the game. You will need to absorb trees and place blocks just like in Arcade, but you'll need to be far more mindful of your energy use and re-absorption. As you may derive from the title, KOTH, is a game where you become King of the Hill. The cyclopic black tower in the center of every level is The KOTH. You must slay the creature by absorption and then replace it to win. This is why I think of it as a single-piece chess game as you move your character across a chess-board like environment with strategically raised plateau and layers. KOTH watches the outstretching board with a beam that destroys artificial structures you place, while leaving trees unharmed. If the beam touches you, you die. You'll respawn where you started, however, anything you collected along the way will be gone. I absolutely recommend checking out KOTH. If you're a casual player, completionist, speedrunner, or VR-enthusiast looking for an odd title to conquer, KOTH has something for you.
label: recommended
annotation_note: 체스처럼 전략적인 핵심 플레이와 두 가지 모드, 여러 유형의 플레이 동기, 적절한 도전성을 긍정적으로 평가함.

review_text_clean: This is a pretty good route for TS. It's not the best and it has its good and band points, but overall it's OK. The scenery and modelling is well done and is probably the best part of the addon. The West London Line is very well done and I use the line a lot in real life, and I have to say, it couldn't be much more accurate in this addon. The trains on the other hand, aren't so good. The class 375 is a good train, but the sounds are pretty bad. The door sounds are completely out of sync with the animations, not that this is uncommon for DTG addons... The sounds also take for ever to catch up when you go to a different view. Also, the cab is very generic and pretty much looks like it has been copied and pasted from all the other units that look similar from the outside. Some of the platforms are bugged, because when I stop the train sometimes, the doors in the first or last units do not open, even though I have stopped well within the middle of the platform. The class 170 is OK, but the sounds are not very accurate and acceleration tend to be slow. I have also found that they have chosen to include hardly any scenarios on the North London Line. All of them are on the GOBLIN. I think there is only one scenario which transversely the NLL. Personally for the expensive price, I would have liked to have seen some more scenarios for this part of the route. Why couldn't they have compiled some over from the old North London Line DLC? Anyway, overall I think the route is good, but the trains not so much. I feel that it may be a bit overpriced for what you get, and a lack of scenarios, so wait for a sale before buying it.

The cons: sometimes the enemies will lay on the ground but still shoot, they hobble around too much for the sniper to be much use, there's only one enemy model (three or four if you count the machines), there are loads of enemies in long hallways, this looks like it was made in 2004, and the AI can be exploited. The game is programmed to run when you call a pass defense, and pass when you call a run defense. On offense it runs out of pass formations routinely--especially when you call pass--and passes out of obvious run formations at least 50% of the time, unless you call a pass defense, of course Computer teams can run any running play out of an empty backfield, for instance, but a human player can run only a reverse. Computer teams can designate the HB hot receiver as primary receiver on long passes, but human coaches cannot. There are dozens of ways the developer figured out to screw you out of most anything you accomplish, and this seems to have been his main focus throughout the game. The game quite obviously runs on profiles, the developer made all of them, and a simple algorithm decides whether or not you win the game regardless of what you do as human coach. Might have been nice if the developer had actually watched a football game before he decided to design one. Alas, he clearly believes the point of the game is to manipulate the outcome artificially, primarily with turnovers and penalties but also with a huge array of artificial means wherever the developer's algorithm determines a timely monkey wrench is called for. The saddest thing about this game is how predictable it is. You can quite literally call most penalties and turnovers before they happen due to the developer's lack of imagination and his determination to manipulate the outcome of games.

I love economic games, territory expansion seems fun, I'm a huge fan of board games, however this does not deliver on any hopes of mine. Perhaps it's because I played a single game against the AI? On the third or forth turn of that game I had enough money to buy all the land surrounding the AI, thus essentially winning the game. The 'tutorial' doesn't explain the game to you. It doesn't tell you what the end-goal is. It doesn't describe the relationship between "P bucks" and actual money. And it doesn't give you any heads up about buildings randomly breaking and needing repair. By the way, you have to right-click them to repair them. Also, you can upgrade them the same way - this was also not explained. There is a lot to be desired regarding quality of life. There's no option to buy territory in bulk - you have to painstakingly click on each tile one by one. There's no information on how many of each type of building you have, or how much production of each resource you should expect. There's no indication of what buying/selling resources will do to the price of those resources - which means if you bulk-sell resources you may end up with less money than you hoped (although I'm not sure if you get paid out the full amount or if inflation hits while you're bulk-selling, there's no indication of which happens). This game is not ready for early access. I do not recommend it in its current state. I am not hopeful that this extremely basic game will grow into something worth playing, but I hope it does.

review_text_clean: I am halfway through the career scenarios and I must say I am really enjoying the route. The route is beautiful with a great mix of cities, small towns, and rural areas. There are several unique assets, and most have winterization applied. There is a lot of rolling stock, including boxcars, hoppers, flatcars, tankers, and gondolas for hauling a variety of different freight. Many of these come in multiple liveries, including NYC, NH, PRR, and BA. There are passenger coaches and baggage cars in NYC and NH liveries. There are plenty of duties for each of the four locomotives that are provided with the route. According to many reviews, the RS3 is completely broken because it has a headlight issue where both the front and rear headlights are always on. While I have noticed this issue as well, it isn’t a major deal and will likely get fixed relatively soon. The locomotive appearances aren’t amazing but not bad either. These aren’t Searchlight Simulations quality, but they aren’t advertised as such either. For the most part, the physics and breaking systems run as I'd expect. I cannot comment on the sounds. I don’t know exactly what these locomotives should sound like. So that all being said - yes, I most definitely recommend this route.

review_text_clean: A very nice, very stylish, creative roguelite bullet-heaven game. The game isn't super long, took me about 6 hours to finish, would probably take about 30 more minutes for 100% of the achievements. The game has full controller support and nice accessibility options for modulating difficulty, not to mention the ability to pick your difficulty less directly within runs as well. The art is great (gives me Cowboy Bebop vibes, can't quite put my finger on why), the music is great, the story (surprised me that there was any!) is basic but touching, the gameplay is somewhat innovative (mixing Necrodancer-style rhythm-combat mechanics with Vampire Survivors-like top-down bullet-heaven combat) and is pretty fun, although it gets a little bit repetitive by the end. I hope there is a bit more exploration of unsteady rhythms if the devs ever make a next entry, there is a lot of leniency in getting 'perfect's here and after a while the consistent rhythm gets pretty second-nature, so it might be nice to see that shaken up. The game lacks polish, but not in any way that truly breaks the experience. It's mostly observed in some unintended behaviours¹, incorrect tooltips, etc. The main thing that diminishes the experience in my opinion is the lack of visual clarity on some levels and with some builds (looking at you, 'Chain projectiles'). I also think it would benefit from some more clarity on how its basic mechanics work (tagging weapons with their damage types, an option to show values in skill descriptions, etc.), the 15 tips on pause help but don't really explain everything (although with how short the experience is and with how not-that-difficult even the later stages are, you won't play for long enough for this lack of knowledge to sour your experience like it probably would in a 100+ hour game). Ah, also, for whatever reason, achievements aren't working at all for me (they don't even show up on the game's page in my library), although that might be Steam's fault. Overall, I'd recommend the game, and also wish the best for the devs in their future endeavours! ¹ = Restarting a run will start you with a random character, including ones that you have not unlocked yet (including the secret 13th, happened on my first death lol). Sometimes the solo that gets activated seems to be random if you have 3 instruments and all have full meter. Using a solo sometimes allows enemies to fire projectiles after all the existing projectiles are cleared, meaning you can get locked into getting hit since you can't move during the solo animation (died to that once :'D). You can actually move during the solo animation, as well as the post-battle "Kill the music" transition, if you were ending a dodge while entering those states. On controller, pausing on the item upgrade screen will pick whatever upgrade you were hovering when the game is unpaused.

review_text_clean: PROS: - Very complex language with many features - expandable with C++ code and DLLs CONS: - Documentation varies from good to not followable and plain incorrect - Examples in the IDE don't even know how to use the poorly documented functions, errors on import - Tiny community, hard to get questions answered - IDE is extremely basic, notepad++ has things over this - Language follows the old BASIC formatting and style to the letter, making it feel very dated Summary: This for me was not worth $50, I would not pay over $20 for this unfortunately. I like older style programming (I write in everything from COBOL to HTML to Java at work) but for how feature rich this language is the documentation really killed it for me. The IDE was another pain point missing many nice keyboard shortcuts and formatting help. I refunded this but maybe might pick it up again if I see changes. I think GLBasic could take some real pointers from AGK on it's documentation (AGK has glorious documentation) and compared to AGK the only thing this has is inline C++ over it (to which I have no idea how far that support goes since this is not a OO language, nor do I think it supports threads which is a big part of C++). Because of this I do not recommend this software :(
